[4] Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) | Sebastian Raschka, PhD
URL: https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/gqa
# Grouped-Query Attention (GQA). Grouped-query attention is an attention variant derived from standard multi-head attention. Instead of giving every query head its own keys and values, it lets several query heads share the same key-value projections, which makes KV caching much cheaper without changing the overall decoder recipe very much. Comparison between multi-head attention and grouped-query attention. GQA keeps the same overall attention pattern as MHA, but collapses the number of key-value heads by sharing them across multiple query heads (Original source: *The Big LLM Architecture Comparison*). In the first architecture comparison article, I framed GQA as the new standard replacement for classic multi-head attention (MHA). The reason is that standard MHA gives every head its own keys and values, which is more optimal from a modeling perspective but expensive once we have to keep all of that state in the KV cache during inference. Memory savings of grouped-query attention versus multi-head attention. Relative efficiency comparison between grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention, and multi-head attention.

[How To Read It In The Gallery](https://sebastianraschka.com/llms-from-scratch/ch04/05_mla/#how-to-read-it-in-the-gallery). Multi-Head Latent Attention is DeepSeek’s answer to the same KV-cache bottleneck that made GQA popular, but it attacks the problem more directly by compressing what gets stored. Instead of sharing keys and values across query heads, MLA compresses them into a latent representation for the KV cache and reconstructs them when needed. ![Image 6: KV-cache memory comparison for MHA versus MLA across context lengths](https://sebastianraschka.com/images/books/llms-from-scratch/ch04-concepts/mla-memory.png). That is the key mental model: MLA is not “shared heads.” It is “compressed cache state.”. During inference, the model stores the compressed latent tensors in the cache and reconstructs the usable key-value states from them when it performs attention. content.text:
Short answer: the multi-head *idea* is absolutely still standard — but the classic implementation has largely been replaced by more memory-efficient variants. The core concept survives; the bookkeeping changed.

Here's the key thing for this node: the reason you wanted multiple heads in the first place is so different heads can attend to different things (one head tracks syntax, another tracks coreference, etc.). That motivation is untouched. What changed is the realization that giving every query head its *own* set of keys and values is expensive at inference time — the KV cache blows up. So the variants all keep many query heads but get clever about the K/V side.

The main lineage:

- **MQA (Multi-Query Attention)** — all query heads share a single key/value head. Maximum memory savings, but a noticeable quality hit.
- **GQA (Grouped-Query Attention)** — the middle ground that became the de facto standard around Llama 2 / Mistral. Query heads are split into groups, each group sharing one K/V head. You keep most of the modeling benefit of many heads, cut the cache a lot. Llama 2 70B, Mistral, and many others use this.
- **MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention)** — DeepSeek's newer approach. Instead of *sharing* K/V across heads, it *compresses* K/V into a low-rank latent vector and reconstructs it when needed. Different philosophy: not "fewer heads," but "compressed cache state." This is what DeepSeek-V2/V3 use.

So if someone asks "is multi-head dead?" — no. Every model still has many query heads. The variants are all about how you store and share the keys and values.

One distinction worth keeping straight, since it touches the neighboring node: *why* multiple heads help (representational diversity) is this node's territory, but *how Q/K/V actually get computed* lives in the "Self-attention mechanism" sibling. The MQA/GQA/MLA story sits right on that boundary because it's all about restructuring the K and V projections.

Want me to go deeper on the intuition for why sharing K/V costs less quality than you'd expect — or is the landscape overview enough?

key_takeaways: The core motivation for multiple heads — letting different heads attend to different things (syntax, coreference, etc.) — is untouched and still standard; what changed is how keys and values are stored and shared.
The classic implementation has largely been replaced by more memory-efficient variants because giving every query head its own keys/values blows up the KV cache at inference time.
MQA (Multi-Query Attention) shares a single K/V head across all query heads for maximum memory savings but with a noticeable quality hit.
GQA (Grouped-Query Attention) splits query heads into groups that each share one K/V head; it became the de facto standard (Llama 2 70B, Mistral) by balancing modeling benefit and cache savings.

MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention) from DeepSeek takes a different philosophy: instead of sharing K/V, it compresses them into a low-rank latent vector and reconstructs when needed (used in DeepSeek-V2/V3).
